name: Slit-scan
basis: why: a slit camera records a narrow strip over and over as time passes; how: slit copied into a scrolling strip, rows from different moments
note: Temporal; on a still it scans a moving copy.

lumenary.blurb: The camera trick behind the stargate in 2001 and the finish-line photo: not the whole frame, only a narrow slit of it, taken again and again. Either the slits are laid side by side as the seconds pass, or every row of the picture is taken from a different moment. A still picture is scanned back and forth so you can see it stretch.

facts.era: Finish-line cameras from the 1940s; the stargate of 2001 in 1968
facts.bestOn: Video with a clear direction of movement; bold still pictures

why: An ordinary camera takes the whole frame at one instant. A slit camera looks through a gap a few pixels wide and records that strip over and over as time passes, laying the strips side by side. Whatever is still piles up into stripes, whatever moves is drawn as its own shape, and a runner crossing the line is drawn as an outline of time. When the slit also moves across a still picture, the picture stretches wherever the slit slows down.
how: Choose a narrow slit of the frame: a single column or row.
At a steady rate, copy that slit into a strip that scrolls away, so that the newest slit enters at one edge.
For the time warp, keep a ring of recent frames and take each row from a different age of it.
On a still picture, sweep the slit across it and back, or shear the frames, so that there is something to scan.
Read between two neighbouring columns, so the strip stays smooth.
history: The slit camera was first used to settle photo finishes at race tracks in the 1940s: film moved past a slit aimed at the finish line, so the picture showed who crossed first, with time running along the film. In 1968 Douglas Trumbull used a much larger version to make the psychedelic stargate corridor in 2001: A Space Odyssey, moving artwork past a slit while the camera shutter stayed open. The same trick is now a standard video effect, and finish-line cameras record thousands of lines a second.
terms: A narrow opening that lets through only a strip of the scene.
A picture of the finish line of a race, made with a slit camera so that time runs across the image.
An effect in which different parts of a frame show different moments.
paragraphs: Finish line. The output is a strip with one line per output column (or row), kept in a ring. Each step of dt seconds adds n = floor(r dt) lines, the remainder carried to the next step, where r runs from 60 to 520 lines per second as the speed slider rises, scaled to the picture’s size. A new line is the picture’s colours along the slit at position s, read as a linear mix of the two nearest columns. On a video the slit stays where the slider put it, so every line of a step comes from the newest frame.

With no motion in a still picture, the slit itself is moved, so that the scroll has something to turn into an image: s(t) = c + A asin(0.92 sin(w (t - t0) + 1.3)) / asin(0.92), a triangle wave with rounded ends in which A is 0.46 of the picture and w is set so that the slit crosses at 0.8 of the scroll speed. If the slit and the scroll moved at the same speed the strip would reproduce the picture exactly; a slower slit stretches it, a faster one squeezes it, and one moving the other way mirrors it.

Time warp. A ring of K = 18 frames is filled at intervals of T/18, with T from 0.3 to 2.6 seconds. For each pixel a lag f between 0 and 1 comes from its position: y/H from the top, x/W from the left, the distance from the middle over the half diagonal for the tunnel, or 0.5 + 0.5 sin(pi (1.6 x/W + 2.2 y/H) - 1.6 tau) for the rolling ripple, which also moves with time. The pixel is read from the frames at lag f (K - 1) and the next one, mixed by the fractional part. For a still picture the frames are the same picture shifted along a path by up to 0.1 W, which turns the lag into a wave of shear.

equations.note: The slit swept across a still picture: a triangle wave with rounded ends, where A is 0.46 of the picture.
Picture pixels per strip line: v is the slit’s speed across the picture and r the scroll rate. Below 1 the picture is stretched, above 1 squeezed, and with a negative sign mirrored.
The time warp: F_a is the frame a steps back and f the lag, from 0 to 1.

presets.text: A vertical scroll turns a still picture into a rolling curtain of its own rows.
A slow, wide time warp from the middle makes a tunnel, as in the stargate.
A rolling ripple warp makes a video wave like a flag.
